Perspective: Are Large, Simple Trials the Solution for Nutrition Research?

Nutritional research and policies have been criticized for relying on observational evidence, using self-report diet assessment methods, and supposedly being unable to present a consensus on what constitutes a healthy diet. In particular, it is often asserted that for progress to occur in nutrition science, large, simple trials, which have worked well in evaluating the efficacy of drugs, need to replace most observational research and small trials in nutrition. However, this idea is infeasible, and is unlikely to advance nutritional sciences or improve policies. This article addresses some commonly held and unfounded “myths” surrounding dietary assessments, effect sizes, and confounding, demonstrating how carefully conducted observational studies can provide reliable and reproducible evidence on diet and health. Also, there is a strong consensus among nutritional researchers and practitioners about the basic elements of a healthy diet. To move forward, we should continue to improve study design and diet assessment methodologies, reduce measurement errors, and leverage new technologies. Advances in the field lie in coalescing evidence from multiple study designs, methodologies, and technologies, and translating what we already know into policy and practice, so we can improve diet quality and enhance health in an equitable and sustainable manner across the world.

Understanding nutritional epidemiology and its role in policy

Nutritional epidemiology has recently been criticized on several fronts, including the inability to measure diet accurately, and for its reliance on observational studies to address etiologic questions. In addition, several recent meta-analyses with serious methodologic flaws have arrived at erroneous or misleading conclusions, reigniting controversy over formerly settled debates. All of this has raised questions regarding the ability of nutritional epidemiologic studies to inform policy. These criticisms, to a large degree, stem from a misunderstanding of the methodologic issues of the field and the inappropriate use of the drug trial paradigm in nutrition research. The exposure of interest in nutritional epidemiology is human diet, which is a complex system of interacting components that cumulatively affect health. Consequently, nutritional epidemiology constantly faces a unique set of challenges and continually develops specific methodologies to address these. Misunderstanding these issues can lead to the nonconstructive and sometimes naive criticisms we see today. This article aims to clarify common misunderstandings of nutritional epidemiology, address challenges to the field, and discuss the utility of nutritional science in guiding policy by focusing on 5 broad questions commonly asked of the field.

In no other field of science would this be considered even remotely acceptable, but for whatever reason this specific strain of epidemiologists appear to belive nutrition is an exception.

While he does acknowledge limitations in self-reported dietary assessment and residual confounding, he then treats statistical adjustment and repeated measures as adequate safeguards, despite substantial evidence that measurement error in food-frequency questionnaires and lifestyle clustering effects are structural weaknesses that cannot be fully corrected analytically.

The implicit argument appears to be basically: because RCTs are hard, our own well-conducted epidemiology must therefore suffice for policy. This necessarily collapses the hierarchy of evidence and essentially converts associative patterns into de facto causal claims. Given persistent reproducibility concerns, modest effect sizes typical of nutrition cohorts, and a history of dietary guidance reversals when stronger evidence emerged, I feel it's fair to state that it was a substantive policy error to treat these arguments as a secure evidentiary foundation rather than as provisional interpretations within a field still grappling with unresolved methodological constraints.

Abstract

Background

The role of observational studies in informing clinical practice is debated, and high profile examples of discrepancies between the results of observational studies and randomised controlled trials (RCTs) have intensified that debate. We systematically reviewed findings from the Nurses’ Health Study (NHS), one of the longest and largest observational studies, to assess the number and strength of the associations reported and to determine if they have been confirmed in RCTs.

Methods

We reviewed NHS publication abstracts from 1978–2012, extracted information on associations tested, and graded the strength of the reported effect sizes. We searched PubMed for RCTs or systematic reviews for 3 health outcomes commonly reported in NHS publications: breast cancer, ischaemic heart disease (IHD) and osteoporosis. NHS results were compared with RCT results and deemed concordant when the difference in effect sizes between studies was ≤0.15.

Findings

2007 associations between health outcomes and independent variables were reported in 1053 abstracts. 58.0% (1165/2007) were statistically significant, and 22.2% (445/2007) were neutral (no association). Among the statistically significant results that reported a numeric odds ratio (OR) or relative risk (RR), 70.5% (706/1002) reported a weak association (OR/RR 0.5–2.0), 24.5% (246/1002) a moderate association (OR/RR 0.25–0.5 or 2.0–4.0) and 5.0% (50/1002) a strong association (OR/RR ≤0.25 or ≥4.0). 19 associations reported in NHS publications for breast cancer, IHD and osteoporosis have been tested in RCTs, and the concordance between NHS and RCT results was low (≤25%).

Conclusions

NHS publications contain a large number of analyses, the majority of which reported statistically significant but weak associations. Few of these associations have been tested in RCTs, and where they have, the agreement between NHS results and RCTs is poor.

Is not a caricature, it's history. It's a fact that much of our foundational nutrition policy, such as the lowfat nonsense from last century, was built on exactly the kind of modest, unreplicated observational associations I described, which were treated as if they carried the weight of causal proof. Bradford Hill himself called his 9 “criteria” 9 "viewpoints", and he carefully argued to help distinguish strong causal signals from weak associations, yet key figures in nutrition epidemiology repeatedly acted as if small, noisy cohort findings could justify sweeping policy.

I agree modern frameworks like WCRF and GRADE are superior as they are more structured than the informal consensus of the past, but they still remain fundamentally inadequate for nutrition: relying heavily on the same underlying weak observational evidence, they struggle to account for pervasive confounding and measurement error, and were originally designed for clinical interventions with much larger, more direct effects. Methodological critiques have shown that applying GRADE to complex dietary exposures can overstate certainty and obscure real uncertainty. Even still, acknowledging these frameworks doesn’t erase the historical fact that early nutrition policy often elevated fragile, non-replicated associations to prescriptive authority, and people still attempt to treat small observational signals as evidence to this day.

This is true- and it's difficult to explain why in a single sentence because the terms aren't as simple as they could be. There are many types of sugar, glucose, frucrose and sucrose (which itself is just a pairing of glucose and fructose) are the most common.

Fructose (and therefore sucrose as well) is the one that the body has trouble handling. The biochemistry in the liver that processes fructose turns it into fat, and the process also has a side effect of 1) signalling for your body to hold on to the body fat that it has and 2) create more body fat from the energy available.

So it is no longer completely true to say "a calorie is a calorie" when it comes to determining whether fat will be burned or added. A calorie from fructose will have a much more weight than a calorie from any other source.

And then you have the confusion about high fructose corn syrup (it's sucrose for all intents and purpose), and people believing "real" sugar is more healthy, and you have a lot of reasons people don't understand what's going on.

text:
Concerns about the health effects of ultra-processed foods are growing, as studies increasingly link them to conditions such as heart disease, diabetes, and even early death. But scientists are still debating what’s driving those risks: the nutritional quality of these foods—which are often high in refined grains, sodium, and added sugars—or the industrial processing and additives used to make them.

A new study from researchers at the Food is Medicine Institute at the Gerald J. and Dorothy R. Friedman School of Nutrition Science and Policy at Tufts University, published in American Journal of Public Health, suggests the processing itself may play an independent role. The researchers found that people who ate more ultra-processed foods had worse health outcomes, even after accounting for the overall nutritional quality of the foods.

“The findings suggest ultra-processed-food factors beyond nutrients—such as changes to foods’ cellular structure, loss of beneficial chemical compounds, additives, and chemicals from packaging—may create health risks not addressed by traditional nutrition metrics or policies,” said the study’s senior author, Dariush Mozaffarian, cardiologist and director of the Food is Medicine Institute.

For the observational study, the researchers analyzed data from 10 consecutive cycles of the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) from 1999 to 2018, linked to National Death Index through 2018. Study participants had completed one or two 24-hour dietary recalls.

Using a standard classification system, the team grouped foods based on how they were made—from minimally processed food-based ingredients like fruits and vegetables to ultra-processed products made with industrial ingredients and additives not typically used in cooking. The researchers also rated the nutritional quality of foods using a system that scores foods based on their overall healthfulness. Each participant received an overall diet-quality score based on the foods they reported eating. The team then examined how ultra-processed food consumption was linked to current health measures—such as weight, blood sugar, and cholesterol—as well as long-term risk of death.

For every 10% increase in calories from ultra-processed foods, the researchers found worse health markers. People who ate more of these foods tended to have higher body weight, worse blood sugar control, higher blood pressure, and less favorable cholesterol levels. They were also more likely to have conditions such as diabetes, metabolic syndrome, and cancer and had a slightly higher risk of dying during the study period.

These links remained even after researchers accounted for reported foods’ nutrient quality and the amounts of saturated fat, added sugar, or sodium present in the ultra-processed foods. The patterns were largely the same across different subgroups of people.

text:
I will just recommend everyone to read the actual definition of the NOVA4 category.

Which one? In 2009, Monteiro defined UPFs as extracted ingredients (eg "oils, fats, flours, pastas, starches and sugars") "plus salt and other preservatives" for the purpose of making them taste better.

In 2010, Monteiro defined UPFs as "result[ing] from the processing of several foodstuffs" (as opposed to "the extraction of one specific component [from] a single basic food") and says the purpose is that they be not just tasty but also "durable, accessible, [and] convenient".

In 2016, Monteiro wrote that "Substances only found in [UPFs] include... casein, lactose, whey, and gluten... dyes... flavours, flavour enhancers, non-sugar sweeteners". The purpose was here specified as "creat[ing] products that are ready to eat, to drink or to heat".

In 2019, Monteiro wrote that one can identify a UPF by the inclusion of "at least one item... rarely used in kitchens, or... cosmetic additives" The former includes "gluten, casein, whey protein, ‘mechanically separated meat’, fructose, high-fructose corn syrup, ‘fruit juice concentrate’, invert sugar, maltodextrin, dextrose, lactose, soluble or insoluble fibre" and the latter includes "flavour enhancers, colours, emulsifiers, emulsifying salts, sweeteners, thickeners".

The Nova system is inconsistent across definitions, it's inconsistent even when put into practice by trained professionals, and it doesn't even define ultra-processed foods on the basis of processing!

That depends entirely on 1) your definition of expensive, and 2) the assumption that everyone can buy in bulk and do meal prep.

Sure, you can make it less expensive by doing those things. But you can't make it cheaper than mass-produced junk full of sugar, fat, and preservatives, because you can buy those things in bulk, too.

ihaterobey estimated below that their meals cost $1-3. If we say they average about $2 ($6/day), that's $182 in a 31 day month, which is under the maximum $194 SNAP benefit for one person. (The average one-person benefit, on the other hand, is $134, and not all states have assistance programs for single adults. I have one neighbor with severe epilepsy who gets $60 of food money a month.) I hope that $6 includes spices, olive oil, any snacks, and all those other things you don't have to buy weekly, and that any poor person who wants to start eating healthy has extra money lying around to get started, because in the first month they'd have to buy those more expensive items all at once - and hope they have enough left for everything else. I also hope you're not expecting to shop at Costco or a similar place that requires membership, because that costs money, too. Not to mention, those groceries better be calorie-dense enough that everything you need for a week fits in two bags or a backpack, which is the max you're permitted on public transit, at least locally (cars are expensive). A backpack of hotdogs, cheese, deli meat, flour, canned ravioli, etc is going to get you (and possibly others) through a week+. A bag full of nutrient dense, fibrous, but low-calorie veggies is...probably not, may go bad before you can eat it, and is likely to get squished and bruised as well. Poverty strongly conditions people to seek out calorie-dense foods while not deeming produce worth the money or space. And that adaptation is literally why the SAD evolved to its current state. It's also stronger and more lasting the longer you live in poverty, especially for children - especially for children who aren't explicitly taught otherwise in school or other venues.

And speaking of children, guess what happens when you add members to a food stamp household? The food allowance per person goes down, because they assume you now buy in bulk. If you're already doing that to make healthy eating doable, your costs aren't going to decrease, which means you're suddenly out of money. Another thing that happens as you include more people is you start running out of space in the small fridge/freezer combo that comes with your cheapest-possible-apartment. This means you need shelf-stable food if you want to keep your family fed, and the expensive kind that isn't full of questionable ingredients is definitely out of your price range. Meal prep may also stop being possible at this point, because your freezer is full of $1.50 bags of frozen broccoli - or maybe it isn't, because anything frozen will melt in the hour and a half bus trip between the store and your house.

But let's say you somehow have room to store a week of prepared meals, and talk about meal prep. Of working age adults who experience one year of poverty, half have a disability, and if we look at anything longer term, that number [increases to 2/3.] (https://talkpoverty.org/2014/09/19/disability-cause-consequence-poverty/) Some of those people would be able to prep meals just fine, but many wouldn't. That might look like not being able to use a knife, having an inaccessible kitchen, having OCD that prevents turning on a stove or convinces them anything not in a sealed container is contaminated, chronic pain with severe fatigue, or a million other things. But even those without a disability might be, say, a single mother with two kids and two minimum wage jobs who spends all her limited time off with her kids, sleeping, or running important errands. (The maximum SNAP benefit for a family of three is about $170 per person per month, by the way, but the average is $126. And did I mention that, despite being called a supplemental nutrition assistance plan, those who get food stamps tend to rely exclusively on them for food? Even if your income increases in the future, food has turned into something you feel guilty spending "real" money on. Maybe for occasional luxuries, but people don't usually put vegetables in that category. )

I'm not saying that some people don't use money as an excuse, or that buying in bulk and prepping meals aren't great ways to reduce cost if they're an option. But those strategies aren't a fix-all, either. Please don't be so dismissive of something that is genuinely a major obstacle for a lot of people. Denying a problem isn't going to solve it, but it will discourage a lot of people.

One of the main disfunctions of insulin resistance is broken regulation of gluconeogenesis. In a healthy metabolism, gluconeogenesis is downregulated by insulin (technically, a high insulin/glucagon ratio) as that means that the body has more glucose than it needs and the liver should therefore not create more.

For those who are insulin resistant, gluconeogenesis works all the time, so there is constant extra supply of glucose. That leads to hyperinsulinemia - which makes it hard for the person to access stored fat - and chronically full glycogen stores - which makes it hard for the person to deal with large intakes of carbs.

That is basically why there are only a few approaches that work for type II diabetes; you need one that makes the unwanted extra glucose wanted and gets rid of the hyperglycemia.
